newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Allies pressure Bosnia leaders on peace process.
newsitem.headline: Allies pressure Bosnia leaders on peace process.

text.p: The Western allies launched an intensive campaign on Friday to force Bosnian leaders to put the stalled peace process back on track and bring indicted war criminals to justice.

Taking their toughest position since the signing of the 1995 Dayton peace accords, the Big Powers threatened direct action unless the Balkan country's multi-ethnic leadership stopped internal feuding and complied fully with key provisions of the treaty.
In a sign that patience is wearing thin, British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said sanctions would be imposed "against those who cooperate (with) and harbour the war criminals".
"We want them given up to face justice," he told reporters at a NATO meeting in the Portuguese town of Sintra.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright began tightening the screws in a private meeting on Friday with the three members of Bosnia's rotating presidency -- Alija Izetbegovic, a Muslim, Kresimir Zubak, a Croat, and Momcilo Krajisnik, a Serb.

Albright, who is leading an effort to put pressure on the parties to the Dayton agreement, warned Bosnian leaders they would be denied $100 milliion in International Monetary Fund loans and more than $1 billion in private donations unless they enacted a national budget.
"Everyone here wants to help the Bosnians, but the Bosnians have to help themselves," Albright told reporters.

Representatives from the major powers involved in Bosnia -- the United States, Britain, Germany, France and Russia -- were ready to deliver a toughly worded ultimatum to Bosnian presidents at a meeting on Friday in Sintra.

The outgoing international envoy to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, called it a "very strong message" that "we think they should move faster on a number of provisions," including arms control, the return of refugees and the normalization of civilian life.

Under the Dayton accords, Bosnia is supposed to be a single state with with two separate entities, one for Serbs and the other a Croat-Muslim federation. But Bosnia's ethic factions have resisted integration, and inter-ethnic central government has ignored some of the main provisions of the U.S.-brokered treaty.

NATO officials said Bosnia as well as neighboring Serbia and Croatia would be under increasing pressure to comply with requirements to turn over accused war criminals -- considered essential to rescuing the troubled peace process.
"We will breathe down their necks today, tomorrow and after tomorrow, and they will know it," a senior NATO diplomat said. "Relentless pressure will be applied."

Four years after it was set up by the U.N. Security Council, a special war crimes tribunal at The Hague has indicted 75 people, including former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his army commander, General Ratko Mladic. They remain at large like the majority of other suspects.

Only nine people have been arrested and sent to The Hague for prosecution, including Bosnian Croat prison camp commander Zlatko Aleksovski. Croatia handed him over last month after U.S. threats to block major loans to the country.

Albright, who has lobbied other allies to join the United States in linking aid to compliance with the peace agreement, was expected to press hard on the war crimes issue when she visits Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia this weekend.

The 30,000-strong NATO-led peacekeeping force in Bosnia is not charged with ferreting out war criminals, but U.S. officials have explored the prospects for setting up a special military unit for tracking down indicted suspects.
With foreign forces due to withdraw from Bosnia in June 1998, Washington and its allies are increasingly worried their time for ensuring a lasting peace is running out.

Bildt on Friday expressed concern that the timetable for troop withdrawal was too tight and said he was urging the allies to keep some kind of armed force in Bosnia beyond the current deadline. "We must not allow a security vacuum to develop," he said.
